authority: Leola's Library current Crochet Mastery instructional material

topics.text: Crochet hooks come in different sizes and materials. Hook size affects stitch size and gauge. Common materials include aluminum, steel, plastic, bamboo, and wood. Aluminum is a practical beginner option because yarn generally slides easily over it.
A yarn label is an important project guide. It typically identifies yarn weight, recommended hook size, yardage, fiber content, and care instructions.
There is not one mandatory way to hold a crochet hook. Comfort and control matter. One common method is the knife grip, where the hand rests over the hook similarly to holding a table knife.

The chain stitch, abbreviated ch, is a basic foundation stitch used to begin many crochet projects. A chain is formed by repeatedly yarning over and pulling the yarn through the loop already on the hook.
For a single crochet, insert the hook into the target stitch, yarn over and pull up a loop, then yarn over again and pull through both loops on the hook. The abbreviation is sc.
For a half double crochet, yarn over, insert the hook into the target stitch, yarn over and pull up a loop, then yarn over and pull through all three loops on the hook. The abbreviation is hdc.

For a double crochet, yarn over, insert the hook into the target stitch, yarn over and pull up a loop, yarn over and pull through two loops, then yarn over again and pull through the remaining two loops. The abbreviation is dc.
Crochet patterns commonly use abbreviations. Examples include sc for single crochet, hdc for half double crochet, dc for double crochet, tr for treble crochet, and sl st for slip stitch.

Colorwork introduces additional yarn colors into a project. A clean color change is normally made while completing the final pull-through of the stitch before the new color begins, so the new color is ready for the next stitch.
Stranded or Fair Isle-style crochet carries unused yarn along the back of the work while another color is active. Tension matters so the carried yarn does not pull the fabric too tightly.
Finishing is the final project stage and can include fastening off, weaving in loose ends, seaming pieces together, shaping, and adding embellishments.
A simple scarf is a useful beginner project because it allows repeated practice of foundation chains, turning, and consistent rows of a basic stitch while learning tension control.
